text.p: These are the key facts about Sudan, under attack by rebels who on Wednesday said they had captured or attacked more army garrisons in the east and were advancing on the southern Blue Nile town of Damazin.

POPULATION: 26 million (1993 census), mainly Arab and Nubian in the north and Nilotic in the south. About 70 per cent are Moslem and animists make up about 25 per cent. The Christians make up about five per cent and are concentrated in the south.

AREA: 2.5 million-square-km (967,500-square-miles). Africa's largest country in area, Sudan straddles the middle reaches of the Nile. It is bounded by Egypt to the north, the Red Sea, Ethiopia and Eritrea to the east, Kenya, Uganda and Zaire to the south and the Central African Republic, Chad and Libya to the west.
CAPITAL: Khartoum. Population 3.5 million (1993).

ARMED FORCES: According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, Sudan has an army of 89,000, including 20,000 conscripts. It is armed with a total of 250 T-54 and T-55 tanks. The air force of 3,000 men has at least 60 combat aircraft including MiG-21 and MiG-23 fighters. A navy of 1,000 men based at Port Sudan has three inshore patrol craft and four river patrol boats. It also has a paramilitary People's Defence Force of 15,000 active members and 60,000 reservists.

ECONOMY: Sudan is one of the world's poorest countries. It has modest oil reserves in the south but rebel activity has dented hopes of a petrodollar bonanza. Oil and gold will form for the first time a source of revenue in the 1997 budget, accounting for 3.6 percent and 2.4 percent respectively.

Canada's Arakis Energy Corp. has a $1 billion joint venture deal to develop an oil concession in southern Sudan. The consortium was formed to develop the Heglig and Unity fields, which are estimated to hold 600 million barrels of oil, and build a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea from southern Sudan.

MODERN HISTORY: Egypt ruled Sudan from 1821 until the Mahdist revolution in 1885. An independent Mahdist Islamic state survived until 1898, when an Anglo-Egyptian victory at Omdurman established Anglo-Egyptian rule until independence in 1956.

The military under Ibrahim Abboud overthrew a civilian government in 1958. African southerners, mainly Christians and animists, waged a secessionist bush war against a mostly Arab, Moslem north that claimed a million lives before a 1972 agreement granted the south autonomy.
The architect of that accord was Jaafar Nimeiri, who became president in a bloodless army coup in 1969.

In 1985 Sudan's near bankruptcy forced him to abolish food and fuel subsidies and a rise in bread prices triggered riots and strikes. In April 1985, while in the United States, he was overthrown in a bloodless coup and went to Egypt in exile.
A Transitional Military Council led by General Abdul-Rahman Mohamed Hassan Swareddahab, which controlled an interim cabinet of civilians, ruled Sudan for a year.

In April 1986, Sudan held elections to return to civilian rule. About 30 parties took part, with the Umma party of Sadeq al-Mahdi emerging as the largest. A national unity government was formed with Mahdi, a direct descendant of the founder of the 19th-century Mahdist state, as Prime Minister.
On June 30, 1989 Mahdi's civilian government was toppled in a coup which placed Lieutanant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir as the head of a military junta.
Influential Islamist ideologue Hassan al-Turabi, briefly imprisoned after the coup, soon emerged as a powerful figure despite holding no official position in Bashir's government.

The United States and Sudan's northern neighbour Egypt, which blames Khartoum for the failed 1995 assassination attempt on President Hosni Mubarak in Addis Ababa, accuse Sudan of training Moslem militants in military camps around the country.

Sudan has accused at least two of its other neighbours, Uganda and Ethiopia, of launching cross-border raids in support of the Sudan People's Liberation Army, which has waged a 13-year insurrection costing more than 1.2 million lives.

Government forces, after losing control of all but a handful of garrison towns in the south by 1991, clawed back territory from the rebel SPLA, which was weakened by internal splits and a loss of foreign support.
But rebels hit back late in 1995 after a two-month ceasefire negotiated by former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, reporting fighting close to government-held Juba, the main southern city.
Human rights groups have reported widescale abuses by both sides, including kidnapping of children into army training.
